Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas · Conversation, family & daily routines

trouble noun and verb

bother, inconvenience

also bother, sorry to trouble you, if it’s no trouble, no trouble, nuisance, be a nuisance, stop bothering me!, inconvenience, if it is no trouble, don’t bother me, get off my case!, pain in the neck, stop being a pain in the neck, don’t be a nuisance

classical

Cic. Fam. 9.25.3: molestiā Fadium līberā
Traupman 398: molestiam gravem alicui exhibēre, to cause someone big trouble

molestia, molestiae f.

noun, first declension

trouble, bother, annoyance

Other words

  • molestus esse — be a nuisance, trouble (someone)

    phrase: molestus agreeing with the subject, with the dative of the person troubled · classical · Cic. Att. 7.7.3: nē molestus familiae veniam; Plaut. Men. 627: Potin' ut mihi molestus nē sīs?

    “Stop bothering me!” is comic: Molestus nē sīs! (Plaut. Most. 74, 601; Men. 250), Potin' ut mihi molestus nē sīs?

  • nisi molestum est — if it’s no trouble, if you don’t mind

    phrase, with a request (velim and the subjunctive) · also used · classical · Cic. Rep. 1.46: nisi molestum est, … velim scīre; Cic. Acad. 1.14: renovārī ā tē, nisi molestum est, velim

    Also ubi molestum nōn erit, when it’s no trouble (Ter. Eun. 483); Traupman (p. 110) gives sī grave nōn erit. Without any trouble: nūllō negōtiō (see problem).

  • sī (tibi) grave nōn erit — if it is no trouble (to you)

    also used · classical · Cic. Fam. 13.73.2: velim, sī tibi grave nōn erit, mē certiōrem faciās (Lewis & Short s.v. gravis); Traupman 110

    Literally “if it will not be heavy for you”: Cicero’s way of putting a request in a letter.

  • Molestus nē sīs! — don’t be a nuisance! stop being a pain in the neck!

    nē with the perfect or present subjunctive: a prohibition; molesta to a girl · also used · classical · Plaut. As. 2.4.63: abscēde hinc, molestus nē sīs! (Lewis & Short s.v. molestus); Plaut. Aul. 3.3.11: molestus nē sīs (Lewis & Short s.v. lēx); Traupman 105: stop being a pain in the neck, molestus (-a) nē sīs

    (vōx cōmica: Plaut.)

Examples

  • sed tamen, nisi molestum est, ex tribus istīs modīs rērum pūblicārum velim scīre quod optimum jūdicēs

    but still, if it’s no trouble, I should like to know which of those three kinds of state you think bestCic. Rep. 1.46

  • nōlō eō diē in Albānum venīre, nē molestus familiae veniam

    I don’t want to come to the Alban villa on that day, so as not to be a nuisance to the householdCic. Att. 7.7.3

  • Potin' ut mihi molestus nē sīs? num tē appellō?

    Can’t you stop bothering me? I’m not talking to you, am I?Plaut. Men. 627

  • Nē mihi molestus sīs.

    Don’t bother me.Traupman 94

See also problem, trouble, please.
